title: Repurposed endogenous virus-like vesicles mediate dendritic cell long-range antigen presentation and T cell activation for enhanced cancer vaccination
abstract: Dendritic cells release extracellular vesicles (DEVs) that amplify antigen presentation while incorporating patient-derived, rapidly evolving antigens. By enriching peptide–major histocompatibility complex (MHC) and co-stimulatory ligands orders of magnitude above donor-cell levels, DEVs emerge as potent vesicle-vaccines, although efficacy remains limited by unclear mechanisms. Here we show that dendritic cells repurpose the virus-like retrotransposon-derived Arc gene to generate endogenous virus-like vesicles (VLVs) that predominantly carry peptide–MHC and high-density co-stimulatory ligands, intensifying and extending antigen presentation. Upon antigen exposure, Arc partners with endogenous envelope proteins to assemble VLVs that directly engage T cells and trigger intrinsic adjuvanticity via viral mimicry. DEVs lacking Arc failed to prime antigen-specific T cell responses, whereas Arc overexpression shifted DEVs toward VLVs that trafficked to lymphoid organs, drove rapid CD4-assisted priming and durable CD8-biased memory, suppressed melanoma, and prolonged survival. Our data reveal a viral-mimicry mechanism enabling long-range immune activation and support Arc + VLVs as an antigen-agnostic vaccine for cancer immunotherapy.

title: Atomically resolved exciton emission from single defects in MoS2
abstract: Excitons, bound electron–hole pairs, govern the optical response of semiconductors and underpin technologies ranging from photovoltaics to quantum light sources. In nanoscale systems, the spatial extent of excitons approaches atomic dimensions, yet direct imaging of excitonic processes in real space has remained elusive. Two-dimensional semiconductors such as transition metal dichalcogenides provide a platform where reduced screening, high light extraction and atomically defined defect sites enable the exploration of exciton physics at atomic length scales. However, the microscopic origin of defect-related emission and its variability across samples have remained debated. Here we show that scanning tunnelling microscopy-induced luminescence reveals the atomic and optical fingerprints of individual defects in monolayer MoS 2 . Decoupling the material from its substrate using bilayer hexagonal boron nitride enables the detection of sharp excitonic emission and spatially localized defect emission, which we attribute to free-to-bound recombination ( e ,A 0 ), and map its distribution with subnanometre-resolved fluorescence imaging. We identify negatively charged carbon–hydrogen complexes as the defect species responsible for a ubiquitous defect emission band in MoS 2 . These results provide atomically resolved images of exciton emission in a solid-state material, linking atomic defect structure to its optical fingerprint and establishing a microscopic basis for deterministic quantum emitter engineering in two-dimensional materials.
